THOUGHT: The patient has acute onset confluent erythematous macules with bullae, frank desquamation, and prominent oropharyngeal mucosal ulceration. Skin biopsy demonstrates epidermal necrosis and detachment, a histologic pattern characteristic of severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS)/toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). He recently began care for arthritis — plausibly recently started a new medication (sulfas, allopurinol, certain anticonvulsants or NSAIDs are common triggers) — and denies new environmental exposures. Infectious causes (e.g., Mycoplasma-associated mucositis) can produce mucosal disease but the biopsy favoring drug-induced epidermal necrosis makes a drug reaction more likely. The distribution is limited (upper half of the back only), consistent with limited body-surface‑area detachment (<10%), which fits SJS rather than TEN. Normal CBC/chemistries do not exclude SJS. The tachycardia likely reflects systemic stress/pain. Overall the clinical picture and biopsy most strongly support a drug-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome.

DIAGNOSIS: Stevens–Johnson syndrome (drug-induced), limited body surface area involvement (<10% BSA).
